q-335473.name: Question 1
q-335473.problem:
A wildlife reserve is monitoring the population of a newly introduced species of deer. The habitat can sustain a maximum population of $850$ deer, but the herd is still below this limit. Since biologists began tracking the growth, the population reached $490$ deer on month $4$ and $600$ deer on month $12.$ On what month will the population reach $800$ deer? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the population of deer, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in months.*
q-335473.worked_solution:
The rate at which the population $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the farm, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=850$ deer, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(850-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{850-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{850-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|850-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $850-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}850-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 850-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 850-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =850-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month $4,$ the population reached $490$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(4)=490,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =490 \\ 850-K{e}^{-4k} & =490 \\ K{e}^{-4k} & =360.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on month $12,$ the population was $600$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(12)=600,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(12) & =600 \\ 850-K{e}^{-12k} & =600 \\ K{e}^{-12k} & =250.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-4k}}{K{e}^{-12k}} & =\frac{360}{250} \\ {e}^{8k} & =\frac{36}{25} \\ 8k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-4\cdot (1/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} & =360 \\ K & =360{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} \\ K & =360\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}} \\ K & =360\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ K & =432\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=850-432{e}^{-(t/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)}
$$

Finally, let $m$ be the month when the population reaches $800$ deer. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(m) & =800 \\ 850-432{e}^{-km} & =800 \\ 50 & =432{e}^{-km} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{50}{432} \\ -km & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}) \\ m & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the population will be $500$ deer on month

$$
m=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216})}{\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})}=47.309…≈47,
$$

rounded to the nearest month.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}800-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 800-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 800-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =800-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $3,$ the number of users was $620.$ So, applying the condition $P(3)=620,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3) & =620 \\ 800-K{e}^{-3k} & =620 \\ K{e}^{-3k} & =180.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $9,$ the number of users was $720.$ So, applying the condition $P(9)=720,$ we get

$$

$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-3k}}{K{e}^{-9k}} & =\frac{180}{80} \\ {e}^{6k} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ 6k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4})\end{aligned}

q-335649.html:
Question 3
?

A mountain valley is monitoring the population of a reintroduced elk herd. The valley can sustain a maximum population of 600 elk, but the herd is still below this limit. Since ecologists began tracking the growth, the population reached 536 elk on month 4 and 573 elk on month 10. On what month will the population reach 590 elk? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

Hint: You may assume that the population of elk, P(t), increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t is the time, in months.

a
20th month
b
17th month
c
25th month
d
14th month
e
22th month
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The rate at which the population P(t) changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation dPdt=k(a−P), where a is the maximum population the valley can sustain, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=600 elk, and we have dPdt=k(600−P).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables: dP600−P=kdt∫dP600−P=∫kdt−ln⁡|600−P|=kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have 600−P>0 for all t≥0. Next, we solve for P(t), as follows: 600−P=e−kt−C600−P=e−Ce−kt600−P=Ke−ktP=600−Ke−kt

Note that K=e−C is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month 4, the population was 536 elk. So, applying the condition P(4)=536, we have P(4)=536600−Ke−4k=536Ke−4k=64.

We're also told that, on month 10, the population was 573 elk. So, applying the condition P(10)=573, we get P(10)=573600−Ke−10k=573Ke−10k=27.

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for k: Ke−4kKe−10k=6427e6k=64276k=ln⁡(6427)k=16ln⁡(6427)

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for K: Ke−4⋅(1/6)ln⁡(64/27)=64K=64e(4/6)ln⁡(64/27)K=64e(2/3)ln⁡(64/27)K=64(6427)2/3K=10249

Therefore, we have the following expression for P(t): P(t)=600−10249e−(t/6)ln⁡(64/27).

Finally, let m be the month when the population reaches 590 elk. Then, we have

P(m)=590600−10249e−km=59010=10249e−kme−km=901024e−km=45512−km=ln⁡(45512)m=−1kln⁡(45512).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the population will be 590 elk on month m=−ln⁡(45512)16ln⁡(6427)=16.905…≈17, rounded to the nearest day.

q-344215.name: Question 4
q-344215.problem: A hospital administrator observed that the growth of the number of occupied beds in a hospital is directly proportional to the difference between the hospital’s maximum bed capacity and the current number of occupied beds. Let $H(t)$ be the number of occupied beds, measured in beds, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in years. If the maximum number of beds the hospital can support is $75$ beds, which differential equation could be used to model the number of occupied beds in the hospital? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
q-344215.worked_solution:
The rate at which the number of occupied beds $H(t)$ in the hospital changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum number of beds the hospital can support and the current number of occupied beds. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=k(a-H),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of beds the hospital can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=75\text{ beds},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=k(75-H).
$$

q-344233.name: Question 5
q-344233.problem: A data center initially contains $320$ computers. The number of computers in the data center $C(t)$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t\ge 0$ is the time in months. If the maximum capacity of the data center is $1000$ computers, which differential equation could be used to model the number of computers? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
q-344233.worked_solution:
Since the number of computers in the data center obeys an inhibited growth model, the rate at which the number of computers changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the number of computers in the data center. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=k(a-C),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity of the data center, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=1000$ computers, and we have

$$

Question 5

A data center initially contains 320 computers. The number of computers in the data center C(t) increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t≥0 is the time in months. If the maximum capacity of the data center is 1000 computers, which differential equation could be used to model the number of computers? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
dCdt=k(500−C)
b
dCdt=k(1000−C)
c
dCdt=k(800−C)
d
dCdt=k(1500−C)
e
dCdt=k(320−C)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the number of computers in the data center obeys an inhibited growth model, the rate at which the number of computers changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the number of computers in the data center. Therefore, we have the differential equation dCdt=k(a−C),

where a is the maximum capacity of the data center, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=1000 computers, and we have

dCdt=k(1000−C).
